title: Effect of Peer Feedback on Paragraph Writing Performance among High School Students
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether peer feedback can improve high school students’ English paragraph writing performance and how students feel about using peer feedback in class. The problem motivating the study is that many high school students struggle with writing in a foreign language, and the authors wanted to test whether a structured peer-feedback approach could support better writing outcomes than ordinary classroom instruction.

The intervention centered on training students to use peer feedback during paragraph writing. The experimental group used a peer-editing worksheet and a 10-point paragraph rubric covering task achievement, language use, and organization. Students received training in how to give comments to classmates and revised their writing after peer feedback. The comparison condition was a control group that followed the textbook-based writing instruction and received teacher feedback, although only some control-group papers were corrected as a whole class because of time constraints. The study collected quantitative data through pretest and posttest paragraph-writing scores and qualitative/attitudinal data through a 6-item Likert questionnaire administered to the experimental group.

Participants were 76 tenth-grade students (39 experimental, 37 control) at a single high school in a rural district in Vietnam. All were 16 years old, monolingual, and learning English as a foreign language. The intervention lasted six weekly 45-minute writing sessions over about one and a half months in a classroom setting. Topics included disadvantages of working mothers, characteristics of Vietnamese people, advantages of electronic devices as learning tools, environmental problems, and disadvantages of living in the countryside.

The main conclusion is that peer feedback improved students’ paragraph writing performance more than the comparison condition. The experimental group showed statistically significant gains from pretest to posttest, while the control group did not show a statistically significant improvement. Gains for the experimental group were reported across all three rubric domains: task achievement, language use, and organization. Students in the experimental group also reported generally positive attitudes toward peer feedback, indicating that they found it useful for improving their writing, especially concluding sentences and use of the simple present tense.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group study in grades 10 with a clear intervention, comparison condition, baseline equivalence on the main outcome, and statistical testing. However, it does not report random assignment, effect sizes, or stronger controls for potential confounding, so it fits green rather than blue.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows statistically significant positive effects on paragraph writing for a priority population (high school EFL students), but effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported, limiting confidence about magnitude. As a result, the impact appears promising but remains unclear in standardized magnitude terms.

finding.finding_summary: This quasi-experimental high school EFL writing study found that students receiving trained peer feedback outperformed the control group on paragraph writing after 6 weeks. The experimental group (n=39) scored higher on the post-test than the control group (n=37), M=6.41 (SD=0.80) vs. M=5.07 (SD=0.89), t=6.86, p=0.00, after showing no baseline difference at pretest (4.65 vs. 4.78, p=0.58). Within the experimental group, scores improved significantly from pretest to post-test, M=4.65 (SD=1.06) to M=6.41 (SD=0.80), t=13.75, p=0.00; the control group showed a small non-significant gain from 4.78 to 5.07, p=0.06.
finding.measure: Paragraph writing performance scored on a 10-point rubric covering task achievement, language use, and paragraph organization
finding.std_deviation: Experimental pretest SD=1.06, post-test SD=0.80; Control pretest SD=0.98, post-test SD=0.89

finding.finding_summary: Students in the experimental group reported favorable attitudes toward peer feedback after the intervention. On a 6-item Likert questionnaire administered to the 39 experimental students, the overall mean attitude score was 3.99/5, with item means ranging from 3.79 to 4.26, indicating generally positive satisfaction with peer feedback for improving paragraph writing.
finding.measure: Student attitudes/satisfaction toward peer feedback using a 6-item 5-point Likert questionnaire
finding.std_deviation: Overall SD=0.20; item SDs ranged from 0.72 to 0.92

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to develop peer review and revision-related skills, and students exposed to peer feedback improved across all three writing rubric domains. In the experimental group (n=39), task achievement rose from M=1.38 to 1.79, language from M=1.44 to 2.01, and organization from M=1.83 to 2.63, all with p=0.00, suggesting gains in revision-oriented evaluative and collaborative writing processes alongside writing performance.
finding.measure: Rubric subdomain scores for task achievement, language use, and organization during peer-feedback-supported writing and revision
finding.std_deviation: Task achievement SDs: 0.51 pre, 0.40 post; Language SDs: 0.56 pre, 0.40 post; Organization SDs: 0.50 pre, 0.40 post
